sections.title: How does the Depth of field calculator work?
sections.html:
The Depth of field calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports circle of confusion limit (C) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sensor size and the aperture f-stop); then you type in the print width, the theta, the visual acuity and the standard viewing distance.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Depth of field calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Circle of confusion limit (C)=actual viewing distance ÷ (enlargement factor × standard viewing distance × visual acuity)
Circle of confusion limit (C)=(lens focal length (f) ^ 2) ÷ (focal ratio (N) × (1000 × hyperfocal distance (H) − lens focal length (f)))
DoF near limit=1000 × focusing distance (u) × hyperfocal distance (H) ÷ (1000 × focusing distance (u) + 1000 × hyperfocal distance (H) − lens focal length (f))
Focusing distance (u)=(1 ÷ 1000) × doF far limit × (1000 × hyperfocal distance (H) + lens focal length (f)) ÷ (doF far limit + hyperfocal distance (H))
DoF near limit=-depth of field (DoF) + doF far limit
Crop factor=(12 × the square root of (13) ÷ sensor diagonal)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Depth of field calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the print width, the theta and the visual acuity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Depth of field calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns circle of confusion limit (C), derived from the print width, the theta and the visual acuity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Depth of field calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the print width, the theta, the visual acuity and the standard viewing distance, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter sensor width in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Sensor width opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Sensor width = 0 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Depth of field calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
